body: Trace the **origin and meaning** of the word **'festival'**.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Origin:** from the Latin **_festum_** ('feast') and **_festivus_** ('joyful, festive'), via Old French and Medieval Latin _festivalis_.
>
> **Meaning:** a **periodic (usually annual) communal celebration** marked by **rituals, music, dance, feasting and display**, held to commemorate **historical events**, honour **gods and ancestors**, mark the **agricultural calendar** (harvest), **purify** the community and renew **social bonds**.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Festivals combine sacred (libation, sacrifice, purification) and secular (durbar, entertainment) dimensions; they serve as occasions for stock-taking, reconciliation and planning community development.

## Simplified explanation

'Festival' comes from Latin **festum (feast)**: a **regular community celebration** with rituals, music and feasting.

body: What are the **major festival types** found in Africa? Identify **two agricultural festivals** in Ghana and state one reason for the celebration of one of them.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Types:** **agricultural/harvest** (new yam, first fruits) · **religious** (honouring gods and ancestors) · **historical/commemorative** (migrations, wars, heroes) · **purification/cleansing** · **hunting** · **royal/installation** festivals.
>
> **Agricultural festivals (any two):** **Homowo** (Ga) · **Odwira** (Akuapem, Asante: new yam) · **Kundum** (Ahanta, Nzema) · **Ohum** (Akyem) · the **new yam festivals** of the Ewe and others.
>
> **Reason (Homowo):** the Ga celebrate Homowo ('**hooting at hunger**') to commemorate a past **famine** that was ended by a bumper harvest, giving thanks to the gods and ancestors for food; the ceremonial meal **kpokpoi** is sprinkled for the ancestors.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Many Ghanaian festivals combine categories: Odwira is both a new-yam (harvest) and a purification festival; Aboakyir (Effutu) is a hunting festival; Hogbetsotso (Anlo) is historical (the exodus from Notsie).

## Simplified explanation

Festival types include **harvest, religious, historical and cleansing**. **Homowo** and **Odwira** are harvest festivals; Homowo thanks the gods for ending a **famine**.

body: What is the meaning of **'display of horsemanship'** in the **Damba** celebration?
answer:
> [!answer]
> During Damba (among the **Dagomba, Mamprusi, Gonja** and Nanumba), **chiefs, princes and horsemen** ride **richly decorated horses** in procession and **demonstrate riding skills** (galloping, rearing, charging). It displays the **power, prestige and warrior heritage** of the **ruling class**, for whom the horse is a symbol of **royalty and authority**.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Damba commemorates the **birth (and naming) of the Prophet Muhammad**, blending Islamic and indigenous elements; the horse symbolises the cavalry tradition of the Mossi-Dagomba states.

## Simplified explanation

In Damba, **chiefs ride decorated horses and show off riding skills**, symbolising their **power and royal heritage**.

body: State **two** reasons why **Muslims recite verses** (the _tasmiya_ and _takbir_) over animals they slaughter in religious celebrations (e.g. Eid al-Adha).
answer:
> [!answer]
> 1. To make the meat **halal (lawful)** for consumption, as Islamic law requires that **Allah's name** ('Bismillah, Allahu Akbar') be pronounced at slaughter.
> 2. To **acknowledge Allah** as the **giver and owner of life**, sanctifying the sacrifice as an act of **worship and obedience** (commemorating Ibrahim's sacrifice).
> 3. To ask for the sacrifice to be **accepted** and blessed, and to emphasise **humane, purposeful** slaughter.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Qur'an 6:118–121 and 22:34–37 enjoin pronouncing God's name over sacrificial animals; at Eid al-Adha the meat is shared among family, the poor and neighbours.

## Simplified explanation

Muslims say **'Bismillah, Allahu Akbar'** to make the meat **halal** and to **honour Allah** as the giver of life.

body: Identify **four ways** in which a deceased person qualifies to be called an **ancestor**.
answer:
> [!answer]
> 1. **Lived a morally upright life** (honest, respected, law-abiding).
> 2. **Died at a ripe old age**.
> 3. **Had children** (left descendants to remember and venerate him or her).
> 4. Died a **'good' (natural) death**, not through accident, suicide, or 'bad' diseases such as leprosy.
> 5. Received **proper burial and funeral rites**.
> 6. Was a full **member of the lineage** (initiated, married) and contributed to the community.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Kwasi Wiredu, Kwame Gyekye and John Mbiti note that ancestors are the **'living dead'**, exemplars of moral life who mediate between the living and God; not every dead person becomes an ancestor.

## Simplified explanation

To become an ancestor you must have **lived a good life**, **died old**, **had children**, died a **natural death** and had **proper funeral rites**.
hint: Good life, old age, children, good death.

body: How is the **last stage** of the rites of passage referred to in African societies?
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Death** (with **funeral rites**), the final rite of passage, through which the deceased **transitions from the world of the living** into the world of the **ancestors** (the 'living dead').
>
> In Arnold van Gennep's model, the final phase of any rite is **incorporation (reaggregation)**; for death, this is the deceased's incorporation into the **ancestral community**.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The life cycle of rites: **birth/naming (outdooring)**, **puberty/initiation**, **marriage** and **death**. Van Gennep (_Les Rites de Passage_, 1909) identified the phases of separation, transition (liminality) and incorporation.

## Simplified explanation

The last rite of passage is **death and the funeral**, which makes the dead an **ancestor**.

body: Identify **two** ways in which **ineffective social control** can affect societies in Ghana.
answer:
> [!answer]
> Any two: a rise in **crime and deviance** (theft, drug abuse, violence) · **moral decay** (disrespect for elders, indiscipline, sexual immorality) · **conflicts and disputes** left unresolved (chieftaincy and land disputes) · **insecurity and fear** · **corruption** and impunity · weakening of **community cohesion** and development.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Festivals such as **Apoo** (Bono) serve as mechanisms of social control by allowing people to **publicly ridicule** wrongdoing, including that of chiefs, deterring misconduct and releasing tensions.

## Simplified explanation

Without good social control, **crime and indiscipline rise** and **conflicts spread**.

body: Explain the term **'celebration of life'** of a deceased person.
answer:
**'Celebration of life'** refers to the practice of treating the funeral of a person, especially one who **died at an advanced age** after a **fulfilled, successful life**, as an occasion of **thanksgiving and joy** rather than only mourning.

**Features:**
1. **Thanksgiving for a long and fruitful life:** the family and community express gratitude to God and the ancestors for the person's life, achievements and descendants.
2. **Joyful atmosphere:** recreational music and dance, colourful (often **white or black-and-white**) clothing instead of red and black mourning colours, and feasting.
3. **Recounting achievements:** tributes, biographies and praise songs extol the person's contributions to family, community and society.
4. **Belief in transition to ancestorhood:** death at old age is seen as a **'good death'** and the beginning of life as an **ancestor**, hence a cause for celebration.
5. **Social and family reunion:** relatives from far and near gather, strengthening kinship ties.

**Contrast:** the funerals of the **young** or those who die **'bad deaths'** are marked by **grief**, and celebration is restrained.

> [!answer]
> Celebration of life: a funeral of an elderly, accomplished person treated as thanksgiving and joy: gratitude for a fulfilled life, a joyful atmosphere (recreational music, white clothing, feasting), tributes recounting achievements, belief in a good death and ancestorhood, family reunion; contrasted with grief-marked funerals of the young or 'bad deaths'.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Christian influence ('thanksgiving service') and urbanisation have expanded celebratory funerals; critics point to escalating costs and ostentation, while Akan custom distinguishes **ayie** (funeral) moods by age and manner of death.

## Simplified explanation

A 'celebration of life' funeral **thanks God for a long, good life**: people **wear white, dance and feast** instead of only mourning, because the person is believed to become an **ancestor**.

body: Why do Africans perform **recreational music** during death and funeral celebrations of their deceased members?
answer:
1. **Celebrating a fulfilled life:** for the elderly who die 'good deaths', funerals are celebrations; recreational music expresses **joy and thanksgiving**.
2. **Consoling the bereaved:** music and dance **lift the spirits** of grieving families and relieve sorrow and tension.
3. **Honouring the deceased:** groups to which the deceased belonged (Adowa, Kete, Asafo, recreational clubs) perform in their **honour**; popular songs the deceased loved are played.
4. **Seeing the deceased off:** the belief that the dead **journey to the ancestral world**, and music and dance give them a befitting send-off.
5. **Social solidarity:** music draws the **community together**, encouraging participation, reunion and support.
6. **Entertaining mourners and guests:** funerals are long; music keeps mourners engaged, especially during wakes.
7. **Status display:** the scale of musical performance reflects the **status** of the deceased and the family.
8. **Reaffirming life:** music asserts the **continuity of life** in the face of death.

> [!answer]
> Celebrating a fulfilled life, consoling the bereaved, honouring the deceased (their groups and favourite songs), a befitting send-off to the ancestral world, social solidarity, entertaining mourners during long wakes, displaying status, reaffirming the continuity of life.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Nketia (_Funeral Dirges of the Akan People_) shows that funerals combine **dirges** (mourning) and **recreational** performances (celebration), reflecting a balanced view of death as both loss and transition.

## Simplified explanation

Recreational music at funerals **celebrates a good life**, **comforts the family**, **honours the dead**, **sends them off to the ancestors** and **brings the community together**.

body: In which ways can **funeral celebrations** contribute positively to the **development** of traditional societies in Ghana?
answer:
1. **Social cohesion and unity:** funerals bring together **family members, friends and communities**, strengthening kinship ties, reconciling feuding relatives and building solidarity.
2. **Homecoming and investment:** migrants and the diaspora return home, often **initiating or funding development projects** (schools, clinics, roads) and investing in hometowns.
3. **Economic activity:** funerals stimulate **local businesses**: caterers, drinks sellers, cloth and printing (programmes, banners), coffin makers, musicians, canopy and chair rental, transport and hospitality, creating jobs and income.
4. **Mutual support:** donations (funeral contributions) help bereaved families and fund community welfare; funeral associations act as social insurance.
5. **Cultural preservation:** funerals sustain **traditional music, dance, dirges, cloth (adinkra, kente)** and rituals, transmitting culture to the youth.
6. **Communication and planning:** gatherings offer platforms for **meetings**, information sharing and planning community projects.
7. **Moral education:** tributes highlight the **virtues** of the deceased, encouraging good conduct.
8. **Tourism:** elaborate funerals (e.g. Ghana's 'fantasy coffins' and dancing pallbearers) attract visitors.

**Caveat:** excessive spending, debt and prolonged funerals can hinder development, so moderation is encouraged.

> [!answer]
> Social cohesion and reconciliation; homecoming that prompts migrants and the diaspora to invest in hometown projects; local economic activity and jobs; donations and funeral associations as mutual aid; preservation of music, dance and cloth; platforms for community planning; moral education through tributes; tourism. Caveat: excessive spending.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Studies of Ghanaian funerals (e.g. Marleen de Witte, _Long Live the Dead!_) show both their economic significance and the burden of escalating costs; some traditional councils have regulated funeral duration and spending.

## Simplified explanation

Funerals **bring families together**, encourage **migrants to invest at home**, create **business for caterers and musicians**, **keep culture alive** and help communities **plan development**.
